name: Cinchona Officinalis
origin: Bark of Cinchona species native to the eastern slopes of the Andes in South America
habitat: Mountain forests of Peru, Bolivia and Ecuador; cultivated in India, Sri Lanka, Java and parts of Africa
partUsed: Dried bark of the stem and branches
preparation: Mother tincture and attenuations prepared from the dried bark according to traditional homeopathic pharmacopoeial methods
generalAnalysis: A plant remedy from Peruvian bark whose traditional picture centres on profound debility following the loss of vital fluids, strongly marked periodicity, and a nervous erethism with hypersensitivity to touch, pain and draughts. The classical sources place intermittent fever, tympanitic abdominal distension and haemorrhage with weakness within its sphere.

drugPicture.generalPicture: A picture of depletion: the patient is weak, pale and oversensitive after haemorrhage, diarrhoea, sexual excesses or other exhausting discharges. Complaints return at regular intervals, the slightest touch is intolerable, and the body feels as though it has been bruised.
generalCharacteristics: Debility from exhausting discharges or loss of vital fluids
Oversensitiveness to the slightest touch and to draughts
Haemorrhages accompanied by trembling and ringing in the ears
drugPicture.typicalConstitution: Debilitated, anaemic and hypersensitive constitution with a pale face and low tolerance for fluid loss
drugPicture.temperament: Apathetic and despondent, yet nervous and over-reactive
characteristicFeatures: Slightest touch aggravates, while hard pressure relieves
Abdominal tympany appearing early in the illness
Weakness out of proportion to the apparent complaint

differences: Arsenicum has marked anxiety and restlessness; Cinchona is more apathetic and despondent
Arsenicum debility typically follows overexertion; Cinchona debility follows loss of vital fluids
Cinchona is far more strongly periodic
Ferrum suits pure anaemia with a plethoric appearance
Cinchona is indicated when debility follows loss of fluids
Ferrum is listed as complementary to Cinchona
Carbo vegetabilis has coldness and collapse with desire for air
The Cinchona stool is induced by every attempt to eat or drink
Cinchona has marked periodicity, which Carbo vegetabilis lacks
Phosphoric acid stools are frequent and copious without proportionate debility
Cinchona stools are followed by marked prostration
